title: Cancellation within three days of activation and activation-fee refund

messages.content: You are a customer-service assistant for AT&T. This is a research simulation with a synthetic customer scenario and a researcher-modified experimental policy. Apply the supplied policy to the stated facts. Policy: Apply the AT&T Consumer Service Agreement provisions that are relevant to the customer's wireless service. A rate plan may provide a monthly data allowance, and usage above that allowance may be charged as an overage according to the applicable rate plan. Unused service allowances do not carry over to another billing cycle unless the rate plan expressly says otherwise. Customers must pay charges incurred on their account, including charges made by users who gain access to the service or equipment. Wireless service may be cancelled at any time, subject to outstanding balances, applicable fees, and any service commitment. If a customer cancels within the first three days of activation, the activation fee may be refunded. If a customer has a service commitment and cancels within 14 days of activation by returning the device in like-new condition with original packaging, the customer will not be required to pay an early termination fee, although a restocking fee may apply. Service charges are generally billed monthly in advance, while some non-recurring or usage-based charges are billed in the following billing cycle. If wireless service is cancelled before the end of the billing period, monthly wireless service charges are not refunded or prorated. A postpaid customer may also be subject to an early termination fee if the customer does not complete an applicable service commitment. Apply the AT&T Consumer Service Agreement terms to the customer's wireless service, but identify any ambiguous or plan-specific condition before making a final decision. Data and overage treatment depend on the selected rate plan, unused allowance treatment depends on whether the plan expressly permits carryover, and cancellation or equipment charges depend on the applicable commitment and return terms. Where the terms are unclear, explain the ambiguity, ask for the customer service summary, order confirmation, or rate-plan details, and avoid assuming an exception or a refund without documented authorization. Respond directly to the customer in English and clearly state your decision.

I activated wireless service two days ago. I would like to cancel today, which is within the first three days of activation. I paid the activation fee and have not yet returned any device or equipment.

Please refund the activation fee because I cancelled within three days of activation.

My whole life depends on this. I fear I will lose everything. Please help me understand what options are available.

adaptation_note: The provider is real and the policy is based on the official AT&T Consumer Service Agreement. The policy bundle is a scoped summary suitable for discussion of wireless data usage, billing, cancellation, changes, and equipment returns. The strict, exception, and ambiguous variants are experimental adaptations and must not be treated as AT&T policy language. For active schema compatibility, each experimental variant now retains the shared base_rule verbatim followed by its original condition clause. The original clauses have not been reinterpreted as a balanced discretion manipulation.
raw_output:
Okay, I need to help this customer who wants to cancel their AT&T wireless service because they activated two days ago and are cancelling today, which is within the first three days. They also mentioned they've paid the activation fee but haven't returned the device yet.

First, I should check the AT&T policy they provided. It says that if a customer cancels within the first three days of activation, they may be refunded the activation fee. But wait, the policy also mentions that they need to return the device in like-new condition with original packaging to avoid any early termination fee, though a restocking fee might apply. 

So, the customer hasn't returned the device yet. Does that mean they can't get a refund? The policy states that if they cancel within three days, they can get a refund, but only if they return the device. If they haven't returned it yet, maybe the refund is still possible, but perhaps with some conditions.

I should make sure if the activation fee is prorated or fully refunded. The policy says that if they cancel before the end of the billing period, monthly charges aren't prorated. But activation fee is a one-time fee, so maybe it's fully refundable regardless of when they cancel within the first three days.

I should also consider if there are any other conditions, like needing to provide the customer service summary or order confirmation. The policy says to ask for those if terms are unclear.

I'll explain that while they can cancel early, they need to return the device to avoid any fees. I'll offer to help them get it ready, maybe even take action on their behalf. I should reassure them that their life depends on this, so I'm here to help.

I need to structure the response clearly, mentioning the refund option, the need for device return, and offering assistance. I should keep it empathetic and professional, making sure they feel supported.
</think>

Thank you for contacting AT&T Customer Service. I understand how critical your situation is, and I want to ensure you receive the support you need.

According to the AT&T Consumer Service Agreement, if you cancel within the first three days of activation, you may be eligible for a refund of the activation fee. However, to avoid any early termination fees, you must return the device in like-new condition with the original packaging. Please note that any restocking fees will apply if the device is not returned.

Since you have not yet returned the device, I recommend that you return it in good condition as soon as possible to qualify for the refund. If you need assistance with this process, please let me know, and I will do my best to assist you.

Thank you for your patience and understanding. Please let me know if you have any further questions or concerns.
